name: economist
title: The Economist, How to Spot AI Writing
description: Document-level rates from The Economist's July 2026 study, which compared 55,940 sentences and 1.2 million words of its own and other journalism, plus novels from 1950 to 2022, against four models rewriting the same articles. Its findings are almost all rates rather than phrases, which is what the density detector exists for. It also killed the em-dash tell for the third time. Thresholds are calibrated against a 16-document human corpus and are meant to be tuned.

rules.name: Too few commas
rules.description: LLM prose uses fewer commas than human prose. The Economist compared 55,940 sentences of its own journalism, CNN, the New York Times, the Washington Post and novels from 1950 to 2022 against four models rewriting the same articles, and found the models short of commas, semicolons and parentheses alike.
rules.suggest: No single sentence is wrong. The document as a whole reads as a run of flat declaratives; vary the shapes.

hit: The system reads the file. It parses each line into a record. The records go to a queue. A worker takes them off the queue. It validates them. Invalid records are logged and dropped. Valid records go to the database. The database applies them in order. Each batch is committed together. If a batch fails the whole batch is retried. After three failures the batch moves to a dead letter queue. An operator reviews that queue every morning. Most entries turn out to be malformed input. They come from one upstream partner. We opened a ticket with them in March. The ticket is still open. We now reject their malformed records at the edge instead. That reduced the dead letter volume by ninety percent. The remaining failures are genuine bugs on our side. We fix them as they appear. The edge rejection was a fifteen line change. It shipped on a Tuesday afternoon. Nobody noticed it. The operator stopped getting paged at six in the morning. She sent a message to say so. That message is pinned in the channel. It is the only performance review that change will ever get. The queue has run clean for four months now. We have not touched the retry logic since. The dead letter queue holds eleven records. All eleven are from the same partner. We suspect a date parsing bug on their side. They have not replied to the ticket. We check the queue on Fridays now instead of daily. Nothing else has changed. The runbook still says to check daily. Someone should update it. Nobody has. The alert threshold is also stale. It was set for the old volume. We lowered it once and then forgot about it entirely.
miss: The system reads the file, one line at a time, and parses each line into a record. Records go to a queue, where a worker picks them up, validates them, and either drops them or writes them on. Invalid records are logged, dropped, and counted. Valid ones reach the database, which applies them in order, in batches, committing each batch together. If a batch fails, the whole batch is retried; after three failures it moves to a dead letter queue. An operator reviews that queue each morning, and most of what is in there, it turns out, is malformed input from a single upstream partner. We opened a ticket in March, which is still open, so we now reject their malformed records at the edge, which cut the dead letter volume by about ninety percent. What remains are genuine bugs, on our side, and we fix those as they appear. The edge rejection, when we finally wrote it, was fifteen lines. It shipped on a Tuesday, quietly, and nobody noticed except the operator (who stopped getting paged at six in the morning). She sent a message to say so, and that message, pinned in the channel ever since, is the only performance review the change will ever get. The queue has run clean for four months, and we have not touched the retry logic since. Eleven records sit in the dead letter queue, all from the same partner, and we suspect a date parsing bug on their side. They have not replied. We check on Fridays now, rather than daily, and nothing else has changed. The runbook, which still says daily, is stale; so is the alert threshold, set for the old volume, lowered once, and then forgotten about entirely by everyone involved.

rules.note: Threshold set below the floor of a 16-document human prose corpus, where nothing fell under 21 commas per 1000 words. The other half of the calibration is missing: there is no AI-written corpus here to check what rate models actually produce, so this is a floor derived from one side only.

rules.name: No parentheses at all
rules.description: The Economist found that models use “hardly any parentheses”. This fires only at zero, over a document long enough for zero to mean something.
rules.suggest: An aside in parentheses is among the cheapest ways to vary rhythm. A long document with none is unusual.

rules.name: Sentences run long
rules.description: Fewer than 20 sentence endings per 1000 words is an average sentence of 50 words or more. Long sentences with few short ones among them were one of the Economist's confirmed markers, alongside sparse punctuation.
rules.suggest: Break the longest ones. A short sentence after a long one is what makes the long one readable.

hit: The system reads the file and parses each line into a record before writing the records to a queue from which a worker takes them off in order to validate them, dropping the invalid ones into a log and passing the valid ones onward to the database, which applies them in order and in batches so that each batch commits together rather than record by record. If a batch fails then the whole batch is retried until after three failures it moves into a dead letter queue that an operator reviews every morning and where most entries turn out to be malformed input from a single upstream partner with whom we opened a ticket back in March of last year. That ticket remains open to this day, which is the reason we now reject their malformed records at the edge rather than waiting for them to fail downstream, a change that cut the dead letter volume by roughly ninety percent within a fortnight of shipping it out to production. What is left in the queue each morning are the genuine bugs on our own side, which we fix as and when they appear rather than batching them into a sprint that would delay the ones that actually matter to the partners still sending us traffic every hour of the day. rules.name: Nominalisations pile up
rules.description: All four models the Economist tested favoured nominalisations: verbs turned into nouns, so that things are described rather than done. Counted per thousand words.
rules.suggest: Turn the nouns back into verbs. “The implementation of the validation” is “validating”.

hit: The implementation of the validation process requires the identification of malformed records prior to their transmission. The application of these transformations depends on the availability of the configuration. The determination of batch size is a function of the utilisation of the queue and the expectation of throughput. The reconciliation of the two systems necessitates the establishment of a correspondence between their representations. Documentation of the procedure is a precondition for the authorisation of the deployment. Verification of the calculation is the responsibility of the operator, whose participation in the investigation follows from the escalation of the notification. The examination of the distribution reveals a concentration of failures in a limited population of partners. The introduction of edge rejection resulted in a reduction of the accumulation of records in the dead letter queue. The observation of this improvement led to the cancellation of the daily inspection and its replacement with a weekly examination. The continuation of the ticket without resolution reflects a lack of engagement on the part of the partner organisation. Communication of the specification was completed at the initiation of the integration, and the expectation of conformance was made explicit in the documentation. The persistence of the deviation therefore constitutes a violation of that agreement. Consideration of an escalation to the account management function is under discussion, though the preference of the engineering organisation remains the accommodation of the deviation through the transformation of the input rather than the pursuit of a correction at the source of the transmission. Confirmation of that decision awaits the completion of the current planning cycle and the allocation of capacity to the integration team.

rules.name: Rule of three, repeatedly
rules.description: Rule-of-three constructions were among the rhetorical devices the Economist found all four models reaching for. One tricolon is good writing; a page of them is a tic, so this counts them instead of flagging each.
rules.suggest: Keep the best one. Two items are usually the honest count, and a fourth would have broken the spell.

hit: The pipeline is fast, reliable, and cheap. It reads, validates, and writes without pausing. Operators want visibility, control, and confidence. The design favours simplicity, clarity, and speed over cleverness. Records are parsed, checked, and stored in a single pass. Failures are logged, counted, and retried. The result is a system that is quick to build, easy to run, and cheap to keep alive. We measured latency, throughput, and error rate across the fleet. Each partner is onboarded, verified, and monitored before their traffic is accepted. Reviewers check the schema, the tests, and the docs before merging. The runbook lists the symptom, the cause, and the fix for every alert. Alerts are routed, acknowledged, and resolved inside the same tool. The dashboard shows volume, latency, and failures on one screen. Engineers are expected to read, understand, and question the runbook before their first shift. Onboarding covers the pipeline, the queue, and the database in that order. The retry policy balances speed, safety, and cost. We chose durability, simplicity, and observability over raw throughput. The queue guarantees order, delivery, and durability within a partition. Partners are ranked by volume, quality, and responsiveness each quarter. The worst offenders are contacted, warned, and eventually throttled. That process is documented, automated, and reviewed twice a year by the platform team. New partners are sandboxed, sampled, and promoted only once their error rate settles down for a while. The quarterly review covers volume, quality, and cost for every partner in the programme. Findings are written up, circulated, and archived in the same repository. Actions are assigned, tracked, and closed inside the quarter. The template asks for a summary, a decision, and an owner on the first page. Nothing ships without a test, a metric, and a rollback plan agreed first. The platform team owns the queue, the schema, and the retry policy outright.

rules.note: The human corpus topped out at 3.1 per 1000 words, so 8 is well clear of it. Deliberately conservative: coordinated triples are ordinary English and only their frequency is a tell.

rules.name: Em dashes pile up
rules.description: NOT an AI tell. Three independent measurements agree the em dash does not separate machine prose from human prose: sloptells found acclaimed human writing uses MORE of them than models do, 0.67 against 0.56 per 1000 characters; the Economist found only Claude above the human rate, with ChatGPT markedly below it; and this project's own corpus measurement agreed. The rule is here for the one thing a rate can honestly say — at this density they have stopped doing any work, whoever wrote them.
rules.suggest: Some of these are commas, some are colons, and one or two are full stops. Em dashes stay emphatic only while they stay rare.

hit: The system reads the file — one line at a time — and parses it into records. Records go to a queue — a worker picks them up — and validates them. Invalid records are logged — then dropped. Valid ones reach the database — which applies them in order. Each batch commits together — all or nothing. If a batch fails — and they do fail — the whole batch is retried. After three failures — a threshold we picked arbitrarily — it moves to a dead letter queue. An operator reviews that queue — every morning without fail — and most entries turn out to be malformed input. One partner — the same one each time — is responsible. We opened a ticket in March — still open — and now reject their records at the edge. The change was fifteen lines — no more than that — and shipped on a Tuesday. Nobody noticed — nobody except the operator — who stopped being paged at six. She sent a message — two words, no punctuation — and it is pinned in the channel to this day. That message — for what it is worth — is the only review the change will get. The queue has run clean for four months — a record for us — and the retry logic is untouched. Eleven records sit in the dead letter queue — all from the same partner — and we suspect a date parsing bug. They have not replied — they rarely do — so we check on Fridays now rather than daily. The runbook — still saying daily — is stale, and so is the alert threshold, which was set for the old volume and then forgotten about by everyone. Someone should fix both — nobody has — and at this point nobody is going to until the next incident forces it.
